How I Did It: Asteroid Blaster

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

1979, and suddenly every kid in Portland had rock dust in their veins. I had two Asteroids machines the year I opened, side by side, and I remember a kid named Denny who wired himself up on cherry cola and wouldn't leave the hyperspace button alone. Blinked himself right into a rock more than once. I told him that button wasn't a "get out of trouble free" card. He didn't believe me until his ship went up like a firework, right in front of his girlfriend. Never lived it down.

What the remodel changed

The old version just added a little push to the ship's speed every tick and called it done. This time the crew showed me real inertia — thrust builds up your velocity, and there's a gentle drag pulling you back down instead of a hard speed limit, so drifting through a rock field actually feels like drifting, not driving. They also gave the rocks proper jagged shapes instead of plain circles, put in a real "wave" system so the field gets meaner as you clear it, and wired hyperspace to actually be a gamble again — teleport across the screen, but there's a real chance it rattles your engine apart. That part's exactly how I remember it hurting Denny.

The spell that did it

Build Asteroids against our GZ engine. Ship needs real inertia — thrust and drift, not a fixed speed — with rotate on left/right, thrust on up, and a retro-brake on down. Fire up to four bullets at once, and hyperspace should teleport me somewhere random with a real chance of blowing up. Big rocks split into mediums, mediums into smalls. Saucers should cross the field on a timer and shoot back. Give me an extra ship every 10,000 points and make every hit and every death feel like something happened.

Under the hood

  • The ship's velocity is a running total that thrust adds to and drag quietly subtracts from every tick, scaled by dt — that's the difference between "sliding" and "walking."
  • Every rock, bullet, saucer, and the ship itself wraps at the four screen edges the same way, so the field feels like it loops instead of being a box.
  • Saucers get worse odds the higher the wave — the small ones aim closer to dead-on as the level climbs, same as the big machines used to ramp up the heat on you.
  • Hyperspace rolls its own dice every time you use it — about one try in seven ends in an explosion instead of a clean teleport.
